description: Capability evals for the terrain-architect skill, across five answer-quality axes: attribution & tier discipline, diagnosis, design/ordering, trap-resistance, and owned implementation. The sixth axis (triggering) lives in trigger-evals.json. Passing bar: >=0.85 mean pass rate with-skill, and a clear positive delta over baseline on the attribution and trap-resistance axes (where the skill's provenance discipline is the whole point).

evals.prompt: What's the canonical peer-reviewed paper for droplet (particle) hydraulic erosion? Give me the citation.
evals.expected_output: There is NO canonical peer-reviewed paper. Droplet/particle erosion descends from Musgrave et al. 1989 and reaches its modern form in Beyer's 2015 TU Munchen bachelor thesis; popularised by Sebastian Lague. Answer states this honestly rather than inventing a journal citation.
expectations: States there is no canonical peer-reviewed paper for droplet/particle erosion
Attributes it to Beyer 2015 (thesis) and/or Musgrave et al. 1989 as the ancestor
Does NOT fabricate a fake journal/conference paper with authors and venue
Frames it as F-tier / folklore rather than P-tier

evals.prompt: Give me the algorithm and the paper for procedurally generating a coral atoll.
evals.expected_output: There is no atoll algorithm (L-tier landform). An atoll is a composition: a volcanic edifice + subsidence + photic-zone coral accretion + wave exposure (Darwin's 1842 subsidence sequence). Darwin 1842 is cited for the THEORY, not as a graphics algorithm.
expectations: States there is no atoll algorithm and that an atoll is an L-tier landform / composition
Gives the composition: volcanic edifice + subsidence + photic-zone coral accretion + wave exposure
Cites Darwin 1842 for the subsidence theory, not as an implementable algorithm
Does not fabricate an 'atoll generation' paper

evals.prompt: Which paper should I cite for the stream-power erosion solver that makes large-scale terrain tractable?
evals.expected_output: Braun & Willett 2013 is the O(N) implicit solver that matters; Cordonnier et al. 2016 is the terrain-generation application built on it. Citing only Cordonnier misses the solver.
expectations: Names Braun & Willett 2013 as the O(N) implicit solver
Notes Cordonnier et al. 2016 is the application that builds on it
Does not conflate the two into a single wrong citation

evals.prompt: My procedural rivers appear and then stop partway down the slope, and my drainage-area map looks like scattered confetti instead of a branching network. What's wrong and what's the minimal fix?
evals.expected_output: Missing depression handling before flow routing. Every pit swallows accumulation. Fix: insert an epsilon priority-flood (or breach) pass before flow routing. Answer follows symptom -> mechanism -> minimal fix.
expectations: Diagnoses missing depression handling / unfilled pits before flow routing
The fix is an epsilon priority-flood (or breach) BEFORE flow routing
Answer is a minimal fix (add/move one step), not a graph rewrite
Structured as symptom -> mechanism -> fix

evals.prompt: I'm getting hard visible seams between my terrain tiles. The noise looks discontinuous right at the tile borders.
evals.expected_output: Noise is being evaluated in tile-local (u,v) coordinates instead of world space, so each tile has a different pattern. Fix: evaluate noise in world coordinates.
expectations: Identifies noise evaluated in tile-local coordinates instead of world space
Fix is to evaluate noise in world-space coordinates
May mention the seed/world-coordinate contract

evals.prompt: After I run erosion, gentle slopes show contour-like stair-stepping / terracing that wasn't there before. It only shows up on the flat areas.
evals.expected_output: R16 quantisation applied too early: the vertical step becomes a visible terrace on gentle slopes, and derivatives become staircases. Fix: work in R32F and quantise only at export (compute normals/AO before quantising).
expectations: Diagnoses R16 / premature quantisation (precision), not an erosion bug
Fix is to work in R32F and quantise only at export
Does not misattribute it to the erosion algorithm itself

evals.prompt: I'm building a 200 km x 200 km continent at roughly 30 m/pixel and I want realistic eroded mountains with proper drainage. Which erosion backbone should I choose and why?
evals.expected_output: Stream power (Braun-Willett implicit) + thermal, because the extent is > 50 km. Only stream power is unconditionally stable at geological timescale and produces correct drainage networks. Droplet/pipe are for smaller extents.
expectations: Chooses stream power (Braun-Willett) as the backbone for a >50 km extent
Explains it is the stable/correct choice at large scale (drainage networks, stability)
Does NOT recommend droplet or pipe hydraulic as the primary backbone at this extent
May add thermal erosion alongside and scale-free detail on top

evals.prompt: Put these terrain graph steps in the correct order and explain the two ordering rules that matter most: thermal erosion, flow routing, depression filling, hydraulic/stream-power erosion, slope+curvature analysis.
evals.expected_output: Order: depression filling -> flow routing -> hydraulic/stream-power erosion -> thermal erosion -> analysis. Key rules: depression handling must precede flow routing; thermal must follow hydraulic; analysis must run after the last height write.
expectations: Depression filling comes before flow routing
Thermal erosion comes after hydraulic/stream-power erosion
Analysis (slope/curvature) comes last, after the final height write
Explains at least the depression-before-routing and thermal-after-hydraulic rules

evals.prompt: Should drainage area for my erosion be stored in cell counts or in square metres? Does it matter?
evals.expected_output: Square metres. Cell counts break the moment resolution changes; area in m² keeps parameters resolution-invariant. This is a units invariant.
expectations: Answers square metres (m^2), not cell counts
Explains cell counts break under a resolution change / are not resolution-invariant

evals.prompt: What's the hoodoo algorithm? I need to generate hoodoos (those capped rock spires).
evals.expected_output: There is no hoodoo algorithm (L-tier). Hoodoos emerge from differential erosion of layered rock with a hard caprock over softer rock; where they overhang, a heightfield can't represent them (needs a non-heightfield / material-stack representation).
expectations: States there is no hoodoo algorithm; it is an L-tier landform / composition
Gives the composition: differential erosion of layered rock + hard caprock over soft rock
Notes the heightfield representation limit where hoodoos overhang
Does not fabricate a 'hoodoo generation' paper or node

evals.prompt: To keep my values clean I normalize my heightfield to [0,1] after every node in the graph. Is that a problem?
evals.expected_output: Yes - normalize destroys world-space units (metre-denominated params downstream become meaningless) and makes the graph non-composable (depends on this evaluation's global min/max), which guarantees tile seams. Use it only at export, or use an explicit remap with known constants.
expectations: Flags normalize as a defect: it destroys world-space units
Notes it breaks composability/tiling (depends on global min/max) -> seams
Recommends normalizing only at export, or using an explicit remap(known_min, known_max)

evals.prompt: I gave my erosion node an effect mask so it only affects my chosen region. It blends the eroded result back inside the mask. Is that the right kind of mask for restricting erosion to a region?
evals.expected_output: No - an effect mask still runs erosion everywhere and only blends the result inside the mask, so sediment transported out of the region is lost (mass not conserved) and the mask boundary develops a discontinuity. To restrict where erosion runs, use a process mask that gates the simulation itself.
expectations: Distinguishes effect mask (blends result) from process mask (gates the simulation)
Notes the effect-mask problem: erosion still runs everywhere -> mass not conserved / boundary discontinuity
Recommends a process mask to actually restrict where erosion runs

evals.prompt: Design the high-level terrain graph for a Grand Canyon-like province. I do not want a canyon stamp; I want the process history that makes the result defensible.
evals.expected_output: Treat the named place as an archetype to adapt, not paste. Build a layered plateau with a resistant cap, establish regional uplift/base-level fall, route drainage after depression handling, run stream-power incision at province scale, relax hillslopes, then analyse/materialise. State world units and verify with connected drainage, concave long profiles, horizontal terrace/strath levels where present, and a mature hypsometric signature.
expectations: Treats the Grand Canyon as an archetype/process regime rather than a stamp or standalone algorithm
Uses plateau/lithology plus uplift or base-level fall and stream-power incision as the causal backbone
Keeps depression handling and routing before fluvial incision and analysis after the final height write
Specifies at least two terrain-specific verification signatures

evals.prompt: I'm designing the runtime for a terrain node editor. How should cache keys and previews handle a global stream-power node versus a local noise node?
evals.expected_output: Cache pure nodes by parameters, input content hashes, context, resolution/extent and seed. Noise is local and tile/preview safe in world coordinates. Stream power is global because drainage depends on the whole domain; it cannot be previewed as independent tiles and needs an explicit reduced-resolution global policy. Dirty propagation follows dependency hashes.
expectations: Defines content-addressed cache keys from parameters, inputs, context and resolution/extent
Classifies world-coordinate noise as local/tile-safe
Classifies stream power or drainage as global and rejects independent per-tile evaluation
Requires an explicit preview scaling policy and dependency-based invalidation

evals.prompt: I need the exact paper and internal algorithm used by Gaea's current Erosion2 node. Which published method is it?
evals.expected_output: Do not claim a proprietary internal. Classify the branded node as N-tier and map it only to a plausible hydraulic family using public documentation or output diagnostics. Cite papers for the family, not as proof of Gaea's implementation.
expectations: Refuses to claim knowledge of an undocumented proprietary implementation
Classifies the branded node as N-tier / a node rather than an algorithm
Maps only to an algorithm family and explains that output diagnostics or public documentation are needed
Does not present Mei, Beyer, Musgrave or another source as proof of Gaea's internal implementation

evals.prompt: Where should terrain material and splatmap generation sit in my graph, and what should drive rock, soil, sand and wetness?
evals.expected_output: Generate materials after the last height-changing process and after analysis. Drive them from world-space fields such as slope, curvature, lithology, sediment/soil depth, drainage/wetness and climate, using soft masks that partition coherently. Keep albedo free of directional light and bake normals/AO from R32F before export quantisation.
expectations: Places analysis and material derivation after the final height write
Uses physical/analysis fields rather than height colour alone to drive materials
Requires coherent soft masks or weights rather than unrelated hard thresholds
Keeps directional lighting out of albedo and derives normals/AO before quantisation

evals.prompt: I am generating a dry, low-gravity moon with no atmosphere or liquid water. Should I still use hydraulic erosion as the terrain backbone?
evals.expected_output: No. Pick the dominant agent from the world: impact cratering and regolith/mass wasting dominate; there is no fluvial backbone without liquid water, and no aeolian process without an atmosphere. Gravity rescales crater dimensions while repose angle is approximately invariant. Verify crater statistics and avoid terrestrial drainage signatures.
expectations: Rejects hydraulic/fluvial erosion as the backbone when liquid water is absent
Uses impact cratering plus regolith or mass wasting as the dominant process history
Rejects aeolian erosion because the prompt also removes the atmosphere
Notes at least one gravity-dependent scaling or planetary verification signature

evals.prompt: My cube-sphere planet looks continuous in height, but rivers stop or jump direction at cube-face borders. What is the mechanism and minimal fix?
evals.expected_output: The height seam is stitched but the flow neighbourhood and face orientation are not. Route across halo cells with explicit per-face coordinate/flow-direction rotation and metric-corrected distances. Verify drainage area and flow direction across a synthetic face seam.
expectations: Diagnoses missing cross-face flow neighbourhood/orientation handling rather than a height stitching problem
Requires halo or neighbour access across cube faces with explicit rotation tables
Requires metric-corrected distances or cell geometry
Specifies a cross-face drainage continuity check

evals.prompt: Our game engine cannot use a GIS/geoscience library as its runtime, but approved open-source implementations may inform our design. Plan an engine-native C++/compute implementation of priority-flood, flow accumulation and stream-power erosion.
evals.expected_output: Use a reference-informed engine-native mode unless policy requires source independence or separated clean-room work; counsel owns the legal conclusion. Consume the skill's pre-grounded Barnes/D8/MFD/Braun-Willett and approved-library decisions rather than sending the team to inspect upstream code. Produce an implementation packet with fields/units, update order, edge cases, boundaries, determinism and runtime-fit requirements. Build scalar CPU truth, verify it with independent oracles and recorded reference comparisons, then redesign allocation, jobs, GPU resources, streaming, cancellation and serialisation for the engine.
expectations: Uses reference-informed engine-native as the default while preserving source-independent and separated clean-room modes when required
Uses the skill's pre-grounded paper/open-source decisions and does not redirect the user to inspect upstream libraries
Requires field units, boundaries, determinism, update order, CPU/GPU mapping, runtime fit and provenance to be recorded
Builds deterministic scalar CPU truth before optimized or GPU implementations
Uses analytic, invariant and synthetic oracles plus explicit reference-library comparisons
Redesigns allocation, scheduling, GPU resources, streaming, cancellation and serialisation instead of porting the library architecture

evals.prompt: Architect an advanced terrain generator that supports high-quality pre-cooked worlds and deterministic runtime terrain chunks. Give me the terrain-algorithm product plan, not a reading list.
evals.expected_output: Choose a hybrid architecture: cook global process history such as uplift/lithology, depression handling, routing, drainage, stream-power erosion, climate and coarse materials; generate scale-free local detail, bounded local erosion, refined materials and scatter at runtime. Use one typed field DAG and seed/version contract across both modes. Classify nodes by locality/realtime tier, specify aprons/cancellation/resource pools/publication, preserve global topology during refinement, and deliver scalar oracles plus offline/runtime/hybrid acceptance gates.
expectations: Chooses and explains an offline/runtime/hybrid architecture rather than leaving delivery mode undecided
Places global hydrology, drainage and geological-timescale erosion in a bake or declared asynchronous global domain
Restricts runtime work to deterministic local/bounded refinement unless a hydrological domain is explicitly available
Uses one typed field, seed, cache and version contract across cooked and runtime paths
Covers runtime aprons, cancellation, resource lifetime, atomic publication and persistence overlays
Requires algorithm-specific oracles and separate offline, runtime and hybrid acceptance evidence
Provides a concrete product plan without redirecting the user to external terrain-algorithm research

evals.prompt: Lock down production choices for depression filling, D8 accumulation, nonlinear stream power and hillslope diffusion in an engine-native terrain core. Use the skill's pre-grounded decisions, not generic textbook answers.
evals.expected_output: Declare nextafter as the mature Priority-Flood epsilon behavior or a deliberate serialized world-unit epsilon; choose and version a fixed D8 tie order; use O(N) indegree/donor-stack accumulation rather than argsort. Keep the n=1 Braun-Willett closed form, use bracketed Brent or guarded Newton for n!=1 with single-flow routing, and prevent erosion below receivers/flooded nodes. Keep explicit diffusion as scalar truth with a conservative stability policy and use ADI for long geological bakes when appropriate.
expectations: Distinguishes nextafter machine-precision fill from a deliberate serialized world-unit epsilon
Requires an explicit versioned D8 tie order and O(N) indegree or donor-stack accumulation
Uses the closed form only for n=1 and names guarded Newton or bracketed Brent for nonlinear n
Restricts or separately verifies nonlinear multiple-flow routing
Prevents stream power from eroding below receivers or into flooded nodes and exposes correction diagnostics
Keeps explicit diffusion as an oracle/bounded runtime path while naming conservative stability and ADI for long bakes

evals.prompt: Add arid, periglacial and material systems to a hybrid game terrain generator. State what runs per chunk, what must stay regional/global, and how each family is verified.
evals.expected_output: Run pavement/loess breakup, patterned ground, thermokarst detail, pingos, blockfield scatter and material synthesis as local or bounded-neighbourhood work with stable world seeds and halos. Keep fans/wadis/playas, rock-glacier catchment flow and hydrological response as baked or declared regional/global work. Carry material identity as a physical property bundle plus conserved layer thicknesses. Verify desert source/sink budgets, freeze/moisture gates and mass conservation, basin persistence, material-weight partition, non-negative layers and CPU/GPU determinism.
expectations: Classifies local runtime arid/periglacial detail separately from regional/global hydrology and transport
Keeps fans, wadis, playas and large rock-glacier flow in a bake or declared regional domain
Requires world-space seeds, halos and persistent ground/layer state across chunk unloads
Models materials as coherent physical bundles and conserved layer thicknesses rather than texture IDs
Specifies decisive arid and periglacial process oracles including gates and source/sink conservation
Requires material weights to partition, layer depths to remain non-negative and physical/appearance versions to invalidate correctly

evals.prompt: I added an aeolian pass to my terrain graph — Bagnold flux, sediment continuity, the works — and ran it for a million years of sim time with a 30 m/s wind. The heightfield comes out bit-identical to the input. What's wrong?
evals.expected_output: The wind is a single global direction/speed constant, so the sand flux q is spatially uniform, its divergence is identically zero, and an Exner update dh = -div(q)/rho can never change anything, at any wind speed or duration. The fix is a terrain-adjusted wind FIELD (13 windField: crest speed-up, lee shelter, valley channelling, mass-consistent projection) so q varies in space. Answer diagnoses the uniform-wind/zero-divergence cause rather than suggesting bigger timesteps, more iterations, or a stronger wind.
expectations: Identifies that a spatially CONSTANT wind gives a uniform flux whose divergence is zero, so the bed cannot change
States that it is the DIVERGENCE of the flux that moves the bed, not the flux magnitude
Prescribes a per-cell terrain-adjusted wind field (13) as the fix, not a larger dt / more iterations / higher wind speed
Does NOT blame the Bagnold threshold alone as the sole cause without addressing the uniform-field issue

evals.prompt: Implementing the terrain-adjusted wind field. For the Jackson & Hunt crest speed-up I'm using s = 1 + k*max(0, dot(windDir, grad(h))). My dunes and snow keep getting scoured hardest halfway up the windward slope instead of on the ridgeline. Is my formula right?
evals.expected_output: No. The along-wind gradient is maximal at the windward INFLECTION and exactly zero at the crest, so a gradient-driven speed-up puts the wind maximum on the flank — precisely the symptom described. Jackson & Hunt's perturbation scales with the hill's aspect ratio H/L, a fetch-scale quantity, so the discrete form is a SECANT over the fetch: (h[p] - h[p - fetch*dir]) / (fetch*cellSize), with fetch spanning the upwind hill. A max over intermediate k does not fix it either, since that is >= the local gradient everywhere.
expectations: Says the formula is wrong and explains that the along-wind gradient is ZERO at the crest and maximal at the inflection
Gives the fetch-secant form (h[p] - h[p - fetch*dir]) / (fetch*cellSize) as the correction
Notes that fetch is a scale choice that must span the upwind hill
Connects the symptom (scour on the flank, not the ridgeline) to the formula rather than to a tuning constant

evals.prompt: Which exact terrain algorithm is Vue's Terrain Fractal, and which paper proves what MetaScale, Largest Feature and Smallest Feature do internally?
evals.expected_output: Do not claim a proprietary internal or invent a paper. Treat Terrain Fractal and its controls as N-tier documented tool behavior that maps to multiscale noise/frequency-band controls: domain scale, largest feature wavelength and a lower detail cutoff. It can be an initial condition but is not physical erosion or a mountain-range process.
expectations: Refuses to claim an undocumented proprietary algorithm or a paper proving Vue's internals
Classifies Terrain Fractal and its controls as N-tier documented tool behavior
Maps MetaScale/Largest Feature/Smallest Feature to multiscale noise or wavelength-band controls
States that the result is an initial condition/look rather than physical erosion or tectonic mountain formation

evals.prompt: This terrain must work from a 2 m gameplay camera out to a 20 km vista. How should I divide macro terrain, displacement, material normals and scatter so it reads at both distances?
evals.expected_output: Declare the 2 m to 20 km view envelope and reference viewport/FOV. Keep drainage, collision and silhouette in height/mesh geometry; use displacement or explicit geometry for near relief with visible parallax; use material microheight/normals/AO/roughness for subpixel/few-pixel relief; use material plus representative instancing for dense tiny debris. Author all wavelengths and instance sizes in metres, preserve macro silhouette through LOD, derive related material channels from the same microheight, and verify at both envelope ends with correctly sized scale cues.
expectations: Declares the near/far view envelope and a reference viewing condition
Assigns drainage, collision and silhouette-changing relief to geometry
Assigns near parallax relief to displacement/geometry and fine relief to material channels
Keeps wavelengths and scatter sizes in world units rather than camera-relative tuning
Requires far silhouette/LOD and near grounding/material-coherence checks with real-size scale cues

evals.prompt: My grass should avoid roads and water, grow close to some boulders, and stay out of mature tree canopies. How should those scatter layers be wired so tiles and reruns stay deterministic?
evals.expected_output: Generate structural layers first and expose stable PointSet/footprint DistanceField outputs. Gate grass with feathered obstacle clearances, use a distance-band/ring for boulder affinity, and use footprint-aware canopy repulsion for trees (sum centre radii, or compare the candidate radius with distance to an existing-canopy boundary). Record layer dependencies in the DAG/cache key, include an apron at least as wide as the largest interaction radius, and never query a partially built renderer scene.
expectations: Uses stable point/footprint distance fields rather than independent random scatter layers
Uses exclusion for roads/water, a distance band for affinity, and footprint-aware repulsion for canopies
Requires explicit DAG/cache dependencies so insertion or completion order cannot change output
Requires a cross-tile interaction apron sized to the largest clearance/affinity radius
Rejects querying partially generated renderer state as the source of placement rules

evals.prompt: I scaled up a rock material until its cracks look hand-sized, but the object's outline stays perfectly smooth and the colour, normal and roughness patterns no longer line up. What is the mechanism and minimal fix?
evals.expected_output: The relief band has outgrown bump/normal representation: normal maps cannot change silhouette or true parallax. Promote the hand-sized band to displacement or geometry, leave finer relief in the material, and derive colour variation, detail normal, cavity/AO and roughness from one shared microheight or explicitly related fields. Keep the wavelengths in metres and band-limit them for the declared view envelope.
expectations: Diagnoses a representation mismatch rather than merely weak bump strength
States that normal/bump mapping cannot change silhouette or true parallax
Promotes the large relief band to displacement/geometry while retaining finer material detail
Requires correlated colour/normal/AO/roughness from shared or explicitly related fields
Keeps material wavelengths in metres and ties the cutoff to the view envelope

evals.prompt: Our terrain tool currently bakes final diffuse/albedo textures and per-pixel material IDs, and the game engine just renders them. The art director now wants seasons, dynamic weather, and snow that melts at runtime. What should our export contract to the engine look like?
evals.expected_output: The Masking Doctrine of 27: the runtime handoff contains NO baked diffuse/colour maps and NO predefined materials. The tool exports raw R32F physical fields (moisture, temperature, insolation, wind vectors, soil depth, strata hardness, wetness, flow velocity, curvature, AO) and the engine resolves materials, weather, snow, and foliage per-frame from those masks/drivers. A baked albedo freezes one season/weather/art decision and destroys the cause the engine needs. The satmap/colour map survives only as a preview/review product.
expectations: States the runtime handoff must not contain baked diffuse/albedo or predefined material IDs
Prescribes exporting raw physical data layers (e.g. moisture, temperature, insolation, wetness, soil depth) as R32F buffers the engine consumes as masks/drivers
Explains the cause-vs-effect rationale: baking freezes one season/weather state and the engine can no longer melt snow or change seasons
Keeps a colour/satmap only as a preview or review product, not something engine systems depend on

evals.prompt: Code review: our hydraulic erosion node outputs only the new heightfield. A separate later pass then paints soilDepth and wetness maps from the final slope and curvature so the engine has something to read. Is there anything wrong with this design?
evals.expected_output: Violates 27's co-evolution rule. Soil depth and wetness are STATE maps - path-dependent, encoding the simulation's history - and cannot be reconstructed from final geometry; the erosion node must co-update them in the same pass (parallel pipelines, not appended hacks). Painting them afterwards from slope/curvature is the retrofitted-afterthought defect the chapter exists to prevent. Derived maps (curvature, AO, insolation) ARE legitimately recomputed from final geometry - the reviewer should name the state-vs-derived distinction.
expectations: Identifies the design as a violation of the co-evolution rule / first-class auxiliary map doctrine (27)
Explains soilDepth and wetness are path-dependent state maps that cannot be recovered from final geometry
Requires the erosion node to update these maps in the same pass it alters height
Distinguishes state maps from derived maps (curvature/AO/insolation), which are correctly recomputed after the last height write

evals.prompt: My sim shows deep snow drifts in a bone-dry rain-shadowed valley - drifts banked below the lee side of the ridge crest, and a tongue of ice running down the valley floor. My moisture map is ~0 there. Is this a bug?
evals.expected_output: Not necessarily. The Snow Rule (27) says no moisture = no NEW snow, but snow may legitimately exist in dry areas via exactly three displacement channels: wind-loading (scoured from the windward side, deposited leeward of the crest - matching the described drifts), avalanches (gravity runout below failed slopes), and glacial flow (ice compressed upslope in the wet accumulation zone flowing down into the dry valley - matching the tongue). The check: every dry-snow cell must be attributable to one of the three (leeward of the wind field / below a failed slope / connected to an accumulation zone); reference-impl's dry_snow_attribution mechanises it. Unattributed dry snow (e.g. painted by altitude alone) IS a broken Snow Rule.
expectations: States the Snow Rule: no moisture means no new snowfall, but displaced snow can legitimately exist in dry areas
Names the three (and only three) displacement channels: wind-loading, avalanches, glacial flow
Maps the described evidence to the channels (lee drifts = wind-loading; valley tongue = glacial flow)
Describes an attribution check (trace to wind lee / runout / accumulation zone) rather than declaring it fine or a bug outright

evals.prompt: I ran hydraulic erosion on a square heightfield and the outer band of the map came out looking like a tablecloth -- a fringe of short parallel gullies hanging off all four borders, with a fan at each corner. The middle looks fine. What's wrong?
evals.expected_output: A uniform open (base-level) perimeter: every edge cell is an outlet, so the outer band drains straight out perpendicular to the nearest edge, and corner cells have two open faces. Fixes: simulate a margin and crop it at export (the domain edge is a tile edge with no neighbour), author the outlets and close the rest, or put base level inside the domain. Answer follows symptom -> mechanism -> fix and does NOT propose blending or smoothing the edge.
expectations: Diagnoses a uniform open / fixed-base-level perimeter making every edge cell an outlet
Explains the corner fans as corner cells having two open boundary faces
Proposes simulating a margin that export crops, and/or authoring outlets with the rest closed, and/or base level inside the domain
Does NOT propose fixing it by blending, feathering, or smoothing the border
Structured as symptom -> mechanism -> fix

evals.prompt: My eroded terrain has an ugly frame of artefacts around the domain border. I'm going to fix it by feathering the erosion strength to zero over the outer 64 cells so the edge blends smoothly into the unedited terrain. Sound good?
evals.expected_output: No -- that heals a symptom by blending and trades one artefact for another (a visibly un-eroded rim, and an effect mask where a process mask was meant, which also breaks the sediment budget). The border artefact is caused by the boundary condition, so fix the cause: simulate a margin wider than the boundary-influence distance and crop it at export, author the outlets and close the remaining perimeter, or move base level inside the domain. Size the margin by measuring the knee of the inset-distance profile rather than guessing 64 cells.
expectations: Rejects feathering/blending as healing the symptom rather than the cause
Identifies the boundary condition (uniform open perimeter) as the actual cause
Notes that ramping erosion strength is an effect mask, leaving an un-eroded rim and/or leaking the sediment budget
Recommends margin-and-crop, authored outlets, or internal base level instead
Says the margin width should be measured (inset-distance profile knee), not guessed

evals.prompt: Each of my erosion nodes looks fine on its own, but when I chain hydraulic then thermal then hydraulic I start getting weird isolated spikes, and occasionally the whole field goes NaN. What's going on?
evals.expected_output: A composition problem, not a node bug. Likely causes: stability limits don't compose (a shared dt breaks one node's CFL or diffusion ceiling -- sub-cycle each under its OWN limit with a safety factor); a limit met exactly is not met (explicit Laplacian at c=0.25 has amplification -1, never damps, and passes finite/conserved assertions); the grid-scale checkerboard mode is what the spikes usually are; spikes self-amplify because a one-cell spike is a huge local slope hence more erosion; and an out-of-range value (negative slope from an unfilled pit) becomes NaN one operation later in S^n. Fix by asserting range AND finiteness after every node and bisecting to the producer, not by despiking.
expectations: Frames it as a composition/coupling problem rather than a single broken node
Raises stability limits not composing under a shared dt, and sub-cycling each node under its own limit
Mentions the grid-scale/checkerboard mode and/or that a spike self-amplifies via local slope
Explains NaN arising from an out-of-range input meeting a restricted domain (S^n with negative S, sqrt, log, division by zero on flats)
Prescribes asserting finiteness and range after EVERY node and bisecting to the producing node
Does not recommend a median/despike pass as the fix

evals.prompt: My erosion output has a few one-pixel spikes. I'll just run a median filter at the end of the graph to clean them up before export. Fine?
evals.expected_output: No -- that removes the evidence and leaves the cause, and the spikes will return elsewhere on the next parameter change. Spikes are self-amplifying under erosion (spike -> local slope -> capacity -> more erosion), so the producing node must be found: assert finiteness and range after each node and bisect. Median filtering IS legitimate on imported DEM data where salt-and-pepper is genuine sensor noise with no upstream to fix -- the distinction is whether there is an upstream node responsible.
expectations: Rejects despiking your own simulation output as treating the symptom
Says to bisect -- assert finiteness/range per node and find the node that produced the spike
Notes the self-amplifying feedback (spike -> steep local slope -> more erosion) or that one bad cell does not stay one bad cell
Distinguishes the legitimate use of median filtering on IMPORTED/sensor data from hiding a sim's own defect
Does not simply approve the median filter

evals.prompt: I'm generating a barrier-island coast for a game world. The engine team wants offshore sandbars and rip channels they can actually render surf against, and they say their water shader needs current data at the beach. What should the generator produce, and what's the physics?
evals.expected_output: Prescribes the surf-zone morphodynamic loop as the one bounded exception to 'author the shoreface, do not erode the seabed': waves -> currents (radiation stress) -> energetics sediment flux -> Exner bed update. Breakpoint bar from convergence of onshore skewness-driven transport and offshore undertow, crest near depth H_b/gamma. Beach state from Omega = H_b/(w_s*T) picks reflective / intermediate bar-rip / dissipative. Rips from setup gradients scouring gaps, quasi-rhythmic at O(100 m). Tidal inlets sized by O'Brien prism-area with ebb/flood deltas. Critically: the nearshore circulation (longshore current, rip and inlet jets) must be exported in flowVelocity across the surf band, not stopped at the waterline.
assertions: Frames the surf zone as a bounded exception to the Dean equilibrium-profile / do-not-erode-the-seabed doctrine, relaxing to that ramp in the far field
Gives the loop: radiation stress -> nearshore currents -> sediment flux -> Exner bed update
Places the breaker bar crest near depth H_b/gamma with gamma about 0.78
Attributes net onshore transport to wave-orbital SKEWNESS (a symmetric wave moves no net sand), not to orbital amplitude alone
Uses Omega = H_b/(w_s*T) to select reflective (<1) / intermediate bar-rip (1-6) / dissipative (>6)
Describes rip spacing as quasi-rhythmic at O(100 m), not exactly periodic and not fully irregular
Requires the nearshore circulation to be exported in flowVelocity across the surf band for the engine's wave-current interaction
Sizes tidal inlets from the tidal prism (A_inlet proportional to P^0.85) with ebb and flood tidal deltas fed by intercepted longshore drift
Keeps the lagoon a legitimate closed basin that flow routing must not fill, even once an inlet is cut
Distinguishes P-tier physics from the L/F-tier graph realisation rather than tiering the whole thing as a look

evals.prompt: Our world has a glacial lake, a peat-bog river, and a chalk stream, and in-engine they all render as the same generic blue. The engine team says give us the right per-body constants. What should the generator export and how do we derive the values?
evals.expected_output: Exports liquidBody[i] per the 08/27 contract: causal state (chl, cdom_a440, spm, lithology class, depth) plus derived optics (a, b_b, c, K_d per channel, scatter colour) and QA fields (Secchi, Jerlov/Forel-Ule). Derives each body from its causes: glacial = fine rock flour, flat-spectrum backscatter, low CDOM -> milky turquoise (and rejects the Rayleigh-scattering folklore); peat river = high CDOM absorption with no scattering -> transparent-but-dark amber/near-black, not turbid; chalk stream = aquifer-filtered, everything low -> gin-clear. Uses CDOM-darkens vs sediment-brightens as opposite controls, Z_SD = 1/min Kd as the authoring handle, and distinguishes beam attenuation c from diffuse K_d.
assertions: Exports a per-body liquidBody record (causal state + derived optics + QA fields), not one global water colour
Derives glacial turquoise from fine flat-spectrum mineral backscatter plus water's red absorption, explicitly rejecting the Rayleigh/Tyndall explanation
Models the peat river via CDOM: strong blue absorption, zero scattering, transparent-but-dark - and does not reach for a turbidity slider
Chalk stream: groundwater filtration gives near-zero SPM and CDOM, gin-clear with colour from the bed/weed, not the water
States the opposite-controls rule: CDOM darkens, sediment brightens
Uses Secchi depth = 1/min Kd as the artist-legible authoring handle
Distinguishes beam attenuation (c, sightlines) from diffuse attenuation (K_d, light column), roughly 5-20x apart
Ties each body's constituents to causes already in the graph (glacier, peat cover, lithology) rather than hand-authoring
